title: Ten-loop fixed-dimension renormalization-group functions of the three-dimensional O(N) model from distributed GPU-accelerated parametric integration
abstract: The renormalization-group functions $β$, $η$ and $ν$ of the three-dimensional $O(N)$ model in fixed dimension (massive zero-momentum scheme) were known to eighth order in the coupling. We extend them to tenth order, and $β$ to eleventh, for general $N$, which requires the two- and four-point functions to ten loops (1,593,254 graphs at the last order), and re-evaluate all lower orders. Through the Callan-Symanzik equation every coefficient follows from per-order sums that are linear in finite, zero-momentum $\bar R$-subtracted parametric integrals, one per graph, which we sample on GPUs by tropical Monte Carlo with densities adapted to the forest terms. The computation reproduces the known sums from two to seven loops within three standard deviations and agrees at ninth and tenth order, at lower precision, with an independent route through an intermediate scheme. The new coefficients have relative uncertainties of a few $10^{-5}$ or better, and the eighth-order coefficients of $η$ and $ν$ improve by factors of 120 and 4. The time needed to integrate an order to fixed relative precision grows by only 2.4-2.9 per loop from seven loops on, while the construction of the integrands still grows factorially and, at tenth order, costs more than the integration. Resummed, the tenth-order series give $ν=0.62997(51)$, $η=0.0333(18)$ and $ω=0.803(14)$ for $N=1$, against $0.62997097(12)$, $0.036297612(48)$ and $0.82968(23)$ from the conformal bootstrap; at $N=3$ the deviations grow, so that the uncertainty is now dominated by the resummation rather than by the coefficients. Every result is generated automatically from, or checked against, a public ledger of independent, exactly pooled runs, hosted on GitHub, to which anyone is welcome to contribute computing time.
summary: This paper calculates the renormalization-group functions for the 3D O(N) model up to ten loops using advanced, distributed GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo techniques. By achieving unprecedented precision in these perturbative coefficients, the authors provide highly accurate predictions for critical exponents. This work significantly advances the theoretical understanding of critical phenomena in statistical field theories.
main_problem:
The paper aims to extend the calculation of renormalization-group (RG) functions ($ eta$, $\eta$, and $
u$) for the three-dimensional O(N) model to very high orders (up to tenth order for $ eta$).
main_result: The authors provide highly precise, high-order coefficients for the RG functions, comparing the resummed series results against those from the conformal bootstrap.
method: The calculation uses the Callan-Symanzik equation, deriving coefficients from parametric integrals sampled on GPUs via tropical Monte Carlo, and comparing results across multiple independent computational routes.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the three-dimensional O(N) model, analyzed in the fixed-dimension, massive zero-momentum scheme, which is a critical system in statistical mechanics.
key_observables:
The RG functions $ eta$, $\eta$, and $
u$, and the critical exponents derived from them.
important_parameters: The dimensionality $d=3$, the number of components $N$, and the coupling constant $u$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the validity of the perturbative expansion and the ability to compute high-order loop integrals, though the authors note the computational cost of constructing integrands grows factorially.
figures_summary: No specific figures are described, but the notes mention Table I summarizing the highest known orders for perturbative RG functions.
paper_structure: The paper details the extension of known calculations, outlines the computational methodology (GPU acceleration, tropical Monte Carlo), presents the derived coefficients, and compares the final resummed results against established non-perturbative benchmarks like the conformal bootstrap.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous, high-precision calculation of critical exponents and RG flow equations provides a benchmark for theoretical methods applicable to quantum critical points in many-body systems.
